what_its_for: Olutasidenib is a cancer medicine used to treat adults with a type of blood cancer called acute myeloid leukemia (AML). It is specifically for patients whose cancer has a certain gene change (mutation) called IDH1, and whose cancer has come back or did not respond to other treatments. Your doctor will test your blood to make sure this medicine is right for you.
how_to_take: Swallow the capsule whole with or without food. Do not crush, break, or chew the capsule. Take it at about the same times each day — once in the morning and once in the evening (about 12 hours apart). If you vomit after taking a dose, do not take an extra dose. Just wait and take your next scheduled dose.
dosing: The usual dose is 150 mg (one capsule) taken twice a day, every day. Your doctor may lower your dose or ask you to stop taking it for a period of time if you have side effects. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions and do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and it has been less than 8 hours since your scheduled time, take it as soon as you remember. If it has been more than 8 hours, skip that missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses at once to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store olutasidenib capsules at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the bottle tightly closed and store it in a dry place, away from light and moisture. Keep this medicine out of reach of children. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about a drug take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking certain medicines that can interact with olutasidenib without first talking to your doctor or pharmacist. These include some antibiotics (like rifampin), antifungal medicines, seizure medicines, and blood thinners like warfarin — your blood thinner dose may need to be adjusted. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice while taking this medicine. Tell all of your healthcare providers about every medicine, vitamin, supplement, and herbal product you take.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you have: fever, chills, or other signs of infection; sudden shortness of breath or trouble breathing; rapid weight gain or swelling; chest pain or fast heartbeat; confusion or trouble speaking; signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or stomach pain; unusual bleeding or bruising; or if you feel very tired or sick. These could be signs of a serious reaction called Differentiation Syndrome, which needs immediate treatment. Also call your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant.
when_it_works: Olutasidenib may start working within the first few weeks, but it can take several months to see the full benefit. Your doctor will do regular blood tests and checkups to track how well it is working. Do not stop taking the medicine unless your doctor tells you to, even if you feel well.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Do not use this medicine if you are pregnant, as it can harm an unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 1 month after the last dose. Men with female partners who can become pregnant should also use birth control during treatment and for 1 month after the last dose. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine or for 2 weeks after the last dose. Liver problems: Your doctor may need to monitor you more closely or adjust your dose if you have liver disease. Older adults: This medicine can be used in older adults, but you may need to be watched more carefully for side effects.
